title: For Nikole Hannah-Jones, a Tragedy; For the Nation, a Catastrophe
author: RHG Burnett
summary: Writing in Education Progress's Attacks on Excellence series, former teacher and administrator RHG Burnett argues that Nikole Hannah-Jones's apology to her daughter is not enough. Because her 2016 essay and later writing, amplified by The New York Times and national awards, shaped how families, educators, and policymakers thought about segregation and school choice, he contends she owes a public correction of the record. He faults the new essay for not reckoning with parents who were pressured to follow her model or who chose differently and were disdained for it. Burnett asks how many failing schools were excused, how many kept open, and how much knowledge children lost because leaders followed her example. His conclusion is that her daughter's harm is a small tragedy, her influence on others a bigger one, and leaving it uncorrected would be a catastrophe.
points: Burnett argues that printing one's diary is not the same as stating what schools and policymakers should do to remedy the damage.
Hannah-Jones herself notes that parents still tell her they made similar school decisions because of her 2016 essay.
He contends her framework cast families who chose alternatives as perpetuating inequality and segregation.
He questions whether she should retain authority in public conversations about how other people's children are educated.
quotes: Hannah-Jones has apologized to her daughter for prioritizing moral convictions ahead of scholastic achievement, but she has yet to apologize to the thousands of parents and children who followed, or were pressured to follow, the model she continued to preach without voicing her doubts.

It is not enough to print one’s diary. The more consequential act, for both Hannah-Jones and the Times, would be to state plainly the steps that schools, administrators, and policymakers can take to remedy the damage their ideas wrought.

Countless families, whether they read The New York Times themselves or encountered her ideas through educators and institutions, came to believe that racism and segregation were the drivers of poor conditions and outcomes in low-income schools.
The public question is not whether her choice served her daughter; it is what happens when one of our standard-bearing institutions transforms a family’s choice into a national educational template.
How many schools were kept open in the name of community identity when they should have been closed for diminished proficiency, inconsistent discipline, or subpar achievement?

It is a small tragedy that her choices harmed her daughter. It is a bigger tragedy that her words pushed others to do the same. It will be a catastrophe if we allow this to go uncorrected and unacknowledged in the future.
